text: “Well!” cried he, throwing his sword upon the bed, “this man must be the devil in person; he has disappeared like a phantom, like a shade, like a specter.” “Do you believe in apparitions?” asked Athos of Porthos. “I never believe in anything I have not seen, and as I never have seen apparitions, I don’t believe in them.” “The Bible,” said Aramis, “makes our belief in them a law; the ghost of Samuel appeared to Saul, and it is an article of faith that I should be very sorry to see any doubt thrown upon, Porthos.” “At all events, man or devil, body or shadow, illusion or reality, this man is born for my damnation; for his flight has caused us to miss a glorious affair, gentlemen—an affair by which there were a hundred pistoles, and perhaps more, to be gained.” “How is that?” cried Porthos and Aramis in a breath. As to Athos, faithful to his system of reticence, he contented himself with interrogating D’Artagnan by a look.
